meta.title: Nonja — a quiet inbox for macOS notifications
meta.description: No banners. Notifications collect quietly in the background, and you read them when you decide to. A menu bar app for macOS.

hero.title: A quiet inbox for macOS notifications
hero.tagline: No banners. Notifications collect in the background, and you see them — grouped by app — only when you open the menu bar.
hero.note: Free and open source. For Apple Silicon Macs.
hero.firstRun: The first launch needs one approval in System Settings

items.title: Collects quietly
items.body: Turn banners off in System Settings and notifications still arrive in Notification Center. Nonja reads them from there and builds a list. Nothing appears over your work.

items.title: Groups by app
items.body: Not one timeline but a bundle per sender, and each bundle's heading clears that app's notifications in a single click.

items.title: Takes you to the source
items.body: Clicking a row does what pressing the real notification does, opening the exact screen it points at.

items.title: Tells you only whether
items.body: A filled mark means something is waiting, an outline means nothing is. No count, so there is no number climbing at the edge of your vision.

screens.list: The mark in the menu bar, with the inbox open beneath it

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.intro: Nonja reads your notifications, so it seems fair to be specific about what happens to them. Short version: they stay on your Mac. There is no server behind this app, no analytics, and no account.

sections.title: Your notifications never leave the Mac
sections.body: Nonja opens the Notification Center database that macOS already keeps on your machine, and it opens it read-only — it can look, and it cannot change anything there. What it reads is held in memory to build the list you see in the menu bar. None of it is uploaded, and there is nowhere for it to be uploaded to.

sections.title: Why it asks to control Notification Center
sections.body: Clicking an item in Nonja takes you to the app the notification came from. Doing that means driving Notification Center on your behalf, which macOS treats as automation and asks you to approve on first use. The permission is used for that and nothing else.

sections.title: Update checks go to GitHub
sections.body: Nonja checks for a new version once when it starts, and never on a timer — an app meant to reduce interruptions shouldn't create its own. The check fetches a small file from its GitHub Releases page, so GitHub sees the request the way it sees any download, including your IP address. Nothing about your notifications is included. It is a plain file download.

sections.title: No analytics, ever
sections.body: There is no crash reporting, no usage tracking, no unique identifier, and no third-party SDK of any kind in the app.

sections.title: You can check all of this
sections.body: Nonja is open source under the MIT license, so none of the above has to be taken on trust. Read the source, or open an issue if something looks wrong.

sections.title: Changes
sections.body: If a future version starts doing something new with your data, this page gets updated before that version ships.
